title: Supreme Court: IBC Appeal Limitation Runs From NCLAT Pronouncement, Not Certified Copy Receipt
meta_description: Supreme Court holds the Section 62 IBC appeal clock starts when NCLAT pronounces its order, not when a certified copy is collected.
bench: Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria
case_name: Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax, CGST Division v. Sreenivasa Rao Ravinuthala and Another
body: The Supreme Court closed out a long-running insolvency appeal on 14 October 2026 without ever reaching the question that started it: whether the resolution plan approved for Samyu Glass Private Limited treated the tax department fairly. Instead, the bench of Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria dismissed the department's appeal at the threshold, on a point of limitation under Section 62 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Chennai, had pronounced its order on 2 August 2023, upholding the resolution plan over the department's objections. The Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax, CGST Division, carried the fight to the Supreme Court, filing its civil appeal on 21 November 2023. Renganayaki Agencies, the resolution applicant and second respondent, raised a preliminary objection: the appeal had come too late.

Section 62 gives a party forty-five days to appeal an NCLAT order to the Supreme Court, extendable by another fifteen days if the Court is satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay. Sixty days in total, and not a day more, is what Parliament allowed. The department's case for timeliness rested on when it actually got hold of a certified copy of the NCLAT's order, rather than on when that order was pronounced. It applied for the certified copy on 6 September 2023, more than a month after the pronouncement, and received it on 11 October 2023. Counting from receipt of the copy, the department argued, its appeal filed on 21 November 2023 was well within time.

Renganayaki Agencies disagreed with where the clock should start. Its position was that limitation, including the fifteen condonable days, ran out well before the department ever filed, counting from the date of pronouncement rather than from whenever the department chose to collect its copy. The Court agreed with that framing. It held that limitation under Section 62 begins to run from the date the NCLAT pronounces its order, and that only the time genuinely required to obtain a certified copy, calculated from when the application for the copy was actually made, can be excluded under Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963, as applied to the Code through Section 238A.

The reasoning turns on what the certified-copy exclusion is actually for. Section 12(2) exists to protect a litigant who has done everything right and is still waiting on the registry to hand over a copy needed to file an appeal. It is not a mechanism to let a litigant sit on an order for weeks before even asking for a copy, and then claim the entire waiting period, including its own delay in applying, as excluded time. The bench reasoned that if limitation only began once a party physically collected its copy, a litigant could simply postpone applying for one for as long as it liked and keep its right to appeal alive well beyond what Parliament fixed. That would make the sixty-day outer limit under Section 62 meaningless, since a party could stretch it just by sitting on the application.

Applying that reasoning to the facts left the department well short. Pronouncement was on 2 August 2023, so the forty-five day period expired around 16 September 2023 and the further fifteen condonable days ran out close to 1 October 2023. The department had not even applied for its certified copy until 6 September 2023, more than a month after pronouncement, and did not file its appeal until 21 November 2023, well after the outer limit had passed even once the time taken by the registry to issue the copy was set aside. The Court held the appeal fell outside the window within which it has any power to condone delay at all.

Having found the appeal time-barred, the bench did not go into whether the resolution plan for Samyu Glass had in fact shortchanged the tax department's claim, or any other ground the department had raised on merits. The civil appeal was dismissed on the preliminary objection alone, and pending applications connected to it were disposed of. Whatever grievance the department had with the resolution plan will not get a hearing in this appeal, strong or weak, because it never got past the gate on limitation.

For insolvency practitioners, the lesson sits squarely on the calendar rather than on the merits of any resolution plan. A party unhappy with an NCLAT order should treat the day of pronouncement, not the day a certified copy lands on its desk, as day one of the limitation period, and should apply for that copy without delay if it wants any benefit from the exclusion at all. The Code already runs on some of the shortest limitation periods in Indian civil litigation, and this ruling confirms that the Supreme Court will read Section 62's sixty-day ceiling strictly, with no room to stretch it by timing the request for a certified copy.
why_it_matters: This ruling fixes how litigants must count the 60-day limit to appeal an NCLAT order to the Supreme Court under Section 62 of the IBC. Parties can no longer extend their effective filing window by delaying their application for a certified copy; only the registry's genuine processing time is excludable, and only once the copy has actually been applied for. Given how often resolution plans are challenged on technical and procedural grounds, insolvency professionals, resolution applicants and government departments alike should calendar the pronouncement date itself, not the date paperwork arrives, as the true start of the limitation period.
card_summary: Supreme Court dismisses a tax department appeal against a Samyu Glass resolution plan as time-barred, holding Section 62 IBC limitation runs from NCLAT's pronouncement, not from when a certified copy is collected.
card_tip: If you plan to appeal an NCLAT order under Section 62 IBC, apply for the certified copy immediately; the 60-day clock starts on the day the order is pronounced, not on delivery.
verification_notes: The case name, citation (2026 INSC 1121, Civil Appeal No. 7882 of 2023), decision date (14 October 2026), bench (Justices S.V.N. Bhatti and N.V. Anjaria), the NCLAT Chennai order of 2 August 2023, the certified-copy application date (6 September 2023) and receipt date (11 October 2023), the appeal filing date (21 November 2023), the limitation holding under Section 62 read with Section 12(2) of the Limitation Act and Section 238A IBC, and the dismissal on the preliminary objection without reaching the merits are confirmed independently by Verdictum, LiveLaw and SCC Online Blog, with the judgment itself available on Indian Kanoon as a primary source. One secondary source stated the appeal was '16 days beyond' the outer limit; that specific figure is not corroborated by a second source and is omitted. The underlying merits of the Samyu Glass resolution plan dispute are not addressed here because the Court itself did not examine them.
